column2: - A file is one module, named on its first line of code. `##` comments describing it may come before.

- `main` lists the capabilities the program needs: here its arguments and the console. They are its whole authority. It can't touch files, the network or the clock, because it wasn't handed them (section 11).
- Blocks open with a keyword and close with `end`. Indentation carries no meaning; `mo format` lays code out with two spaces per level, in lines of at most 100 columns.

A program is a tree of modules under one root folder. The module `Shop.OrderBook` lives in `shop/order-book.mo`: each part of its name becomes a lowercase folder or file name, with hyphens between words. A word starts at a capital letter that follows a lowercase letter or a digit, and at the last capital of a run that a lowercase letter follows, so `XMLReader` lives in `xml-reader.mo`, `HTTP2Server` in `http2-server.mo` and `Unicode16Tool` in `unicode16-tool.mo`.

Source is UTF-8. Characters that change how text looks without being seen are an error anywhere, even in text and comments: direction overrides, zero-width characters, and control characters other than tab and line breaks. In text, write them as escapes, such as `"\u{200B}"`.

`#` starts a comment that runs to the end of the line. `##` documents the declaration below it, or the module when it comes before `module`. `mo format` lines up the comments at the ends of consecutive lines in one column, two spaces after the longest line's code.
- Values, functions, fields and parameters are snake_case: lowercase ASCII letters, digits and `_`, starting with a letter, or with `_` for a name that is unused on purpose.
- Types, the cases of choice types, and modules are CapCase: `OrderBook`, `NotFound`.
- A type parameter is a single capital letter: `T`, `K`, `V`.
- A name ending in `?` is a yes-or-no answer: a `Bool`, or a function that returns one, such as `empty?` or `paid?`.
- `_` alone means "ignored", and a name starting with `_`, such as `_reason`, is unused on purpose.
Names are ASCII; text and comments may use any Unicode. These words are reserved:
allows and assert break case continue else end enum examples expose false fn for forbids if implies in is module not or promise return service stop struct test true try use var where while
`service` is reserved. The service-clause words `state`, `tools`, `every`, `token`, `from` and `env` remain ordinary identifiers outside their clause positions (section 11.5).

A line break ends a statement; there are no semicolons. A statement continues on the next line when its line ends with an opening bracket, a comma, `.`, `=` or a binary operator, or when the next line starts with a closing bracket, `.`, `where` or a binary operator other than `-`. A statement also runs on through any block it opens, such as a `case` or an anonymous function written on several lines, to that block's `end`.

These show where a statement may break. `mo format` chooses the breaks itself: a statement that fits in 100 columns goes on one line, so it would join each of these, and a longer one is broken at its outermost brackets, dots or operators first. It counts columns as `Unicode16.display_width` does (section 14), turns any run of blank lines between statements into one, and writes no trailing commas.
| `Bool` | `true` and `false` | 3.1 |
| `Int`, `BigInt`, `Byte` | whole numbers | 3.2 |
| `Decimal`, `Float` | fractions | 3.3 |
| `Text`, `Char`, `Bytes` | Unicode text, one character, binary data | 3.4 |
| `Unit` | just `Unit`, what a function that returns nothing returns | 3.5 |
| `(A, B)` | tuples | 3.6 |
| `List(T)`, `Map(K, V)`, `Set(T)` | collections | 3.7, 3.8 |
| `Range` | whole numbers from `a` up to `b`, written `a..b` | 7.5 |
| `Time`, `Duration` | instants and lengths of time | 3.9 |
| records and choice types | declared with `struct` and `enum` | 4 |
| `fn(A) : B` | functions | 5.6 |
| `Option(T)`, `Result(T, E)` | maybe-missing values, and success or failure | 8 |
| capabilities | `Console`, `Files` and the others | 11 |

All values are immutable. A `var` (section 6.2) changes which value a name holds, never a value someone else holds. Mo never converts between types silently: a conversion is a function call, and one that could fail returns an `Option`. Conversions that round, such as `to_float` and `to_fixed`, say how they round. Comparing or combining values of different types is an error.
`and` and `or` evaluate their right side only when they need it, and `not` negates. A condition must be a `Bool`: no numbers, texts or lists stand in for one.
`a implies b` means `not a or b`. It reads best in promises (section 12.2).
`Int` is a 64-bit signed whole number, and the type of counts, sizes and positions. Literals may put `_` between digits, and may be hexadecimal or binary:

`+`, `-`, `*`, `/` and `%` take two numbers of the same type. `/` rounds toward zero, and `%` gives the remainder with the sign of the left side: `-7 / 2` is `-3`, and `-7 % 2` is `-1`. `a.floor_div(b)` and `a.floor_mod(b)` round toward negative infinity instead.
Overflow, and dividing by zero, are bugs: the program stops. Code that expects a result might not fit says what it wants instead:

`BigInt` holds whole numbers of any size, with the same arithmetic: `n.to_big` converts to one, and `big.to_int` returns `None` when the value doesn't fit. `Byte` holds 0 to 255, for binary data; `n.to_byte` returns an `Option(Byte)`. `Byte` has no arithmetic (section 9.2): convert it with `to_int` first.

A literal with a decimal point, such as `19.99`, is a `Decimal`: an exact fraction with 18 decimal places, up to about ±1.7 × 10²⁰. Decimal arithmetic is exact while results fit in 18 places, so `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3`. A result that needs more places, such as `1.00 / 3`, is rounded to the nearest 18th place, with an exact tie rounded to the even digit. Overflow and dividing by zero stop the program, as with `Int`, and `%` gives the remainder with the sign of the left side, as it does for `Int`. A decimal's text form is its shortest exact spelling: `15.5`, `3`, `0.001`.

`Float` is a 64-bit IEEE 754 binary floating-point number, for science and graphics. A number literal takes the type its context needs: in `x * 0.5`, with `x` a `Float`, `0.5` is a `Float`, and in `price * 2`, with `price` a `Decimal`, `2` is a `Decimal`. A literal with nothing to decide its type is an `Int`, or a `Decimal` if it has a decimal point. Dividing an `Int` by an `Int` gives an `Int`, so convert first to get a fraction: `total.to_decimal / count.to_decimal`. Converting is explicit:

`Text` is Unicode text. It is stored as UTF-8 and is always valid. Text is written in double quotes, with the escapes `\n`, `\t`, `\r`, `\\`, `\"`, `\'`, `\#` and `\u{1F600}` (a character by its hexadecimal code). `#{...}` inside text inserts the text form of any value that has one (section 9.2), and may hold any expression, even one with text in it, as in `"#{name or "you"}"`. Lines inside `#{...}` break as they do elsewhere (section 2.4), with `#{` and its `}` as brackets, so a `case` may run over several lines there:

Text on several lines starts with `"""` at the end of a line and ends with `"""` first on a line, after its indentation; code may go on after it on that line, as in `""")`. It holds the lines between them, without the line break before the closing `"""`, which sets the indentation every line drops:
A `Char` is one Unicode character (a code point), in single quotes: `'a'`, `'\n'`, `'é'`.

Text has no single "length". `text.byte_count` counts UTF-8 bytes, instantly; `text.char_count` counts characters, reading the text. There is no `text[i]`: use whole-text operations such as `split`, `lines`, `trim`, `starts_with?` and `replace`, or walk `text.chars`. Two texts are equal when their bytes are equal, and texts sort by character code. Mo never normalizes text silently. The `Unicode16` module (section 14) normalizes text, splits it into user-perceived characters, and converts case beyond ASCII.

`Bytes` is binary data. `text.bytes` always succeeds; `bytes.decode_utf8` returns `None` when the bytes aren't valid UTF-8. `bytes.slice(from, to)` cuts a part out, `Bytes.join(parts)` puts parts together, and `Bytes.empty`, `Bytes.zeroed`, `Bytes.from_list`, `to_list`, and the big-endian integer helpers pack and unpack binary formats (section 14).
`Unit` is the type with one value, also written `Unit`. A function with no result type returns it. `Result(Unit, E)` is the result of an action that can fail but has nothing to return.
A tuple groups two or more values: `(3, "three")` has type `(Int, Text)`. `pair.0` and `pair.1` read its parts, and a pattern takes it apart:
`List(T)` is Mo's sequence: `[1, 2, 3]`, or `[]` when empty. Every element has the same type. Reading by position returns an `Option`, because the position may be past the end:

Functions that "change" a list return a new one, so `items.append(4)` on a line of its own is an error: the new list is unused. With a `var`, write `items = items.append(4)`. When the old list has no other holder, the new one reuses its memory, so building a list in a loop costs what it would with a mutable array (section 13.3).

`Map(K, V)` maps keys to values: `{"apples": 3, "pears": 5}`, or `{}` when empty. Keys are expressions, so `{fruit: 3}` uses the value of `fruit`. A literal that gives the same key twice is an error when the compiler can see it, as with two equal literals or the same name twice, and a bug when two keys turn out equal as the program runs. `Set(T)` holds distinct values: `Set.empty`, a constant, or `items.to_set`. Keys and set members need equality and hashing, which most types have (section 9.2).

Maps and sets keep insertion order, also after removals: iterating visits keys in the order they were added, setting an existing key keeps its place, and a key removed and added again goes last. Two maps are equal when they hold the same entries, in any order. Iterating a map gives `(key, value)` tuples.

A `Time` is an instant between the years 1 and 9999, read from a `Clock` (section 11). A `Duration` is a length of time, made from an `Int`: `5.seconds`, `200.milliseconds`, `3.minutes`, `2.hours`, `7.days`. Each unit also accepts its singular spelling: `second`, `millisecond`, `minute`, `hour`, `day`. Either spelling works with any `Int`, including qualified calls and function values such as `Int.minute`. Both times and durations count whole microseconds. Subtracting two times gives a `Duration`, and never overflows; adding a `Duration` to a `Time`, or subtracting one from it, gives a `Time`; durations add, subtract and multiply by an `Int`. A time outside the years 1 to 9999 is a bug, so `time.checked_add(duration)` returns an `Option`, `None` outside them, for code that can't rule it out; a negative duration goes back in time. Times and durations compare with `<` and the other comparisons.

`mo format` writes a singular unit on a direct integer-literal receiver whose value is 1, including hexadecimal and binary literals, and a plural unit on other integer literals. It leaves other receivers and qualified function names as written: `n.minute`, `record.seconds`, `(1).minutes`, `(-1).second`, and `Int.minute`. In `-1.seconds`, the receiver is the literal 1, so it writes `-1.second`. The formatter uses syntax, not types; this boundary avoids renaming unrelated fields or functions.
A `struct` declares a record type: named fields, each with a type. A record is built by naming every field, in any order, and its fields are read with `.`:

When a record is built, its fields are computed in the order they are written there, whatever their order in the declaration. There are no optional fields; a field that may be missing has an `Option` type. Records have no methods: functions in the record's module work on it (section 5.4).
An `enum` declares a choice type: each value is exactly one of its cases. A case carries no data, one unnamed value, or named fields:
A case is built like a record, by naming its fields, or from its one unnamed value: `Circle(2.5)`. Types may be generic and recursive:

A module's cases share one name space: no two of its enums have a case of the same name, and no case reuses the name of a type or case that is always in scope, such as `Set`, `None` or `Error`. `Option` and `Result` are ordinary choice types (section 8).

A signature gives every parameter's type and the result's type; a function with no result type returns `Unit`. Inside a body, types are inferred from all their uses in it. A body is a sequence of statements, and its value is the value of its last line. `return` leaves early. A trailing `if`, a guard, is allowed only on the three early exits: `return`, `break` and `continue`.

Functions are declared at the top level of a module. There are no default or optional parameters. Two functions in a module share a name only when their first parameters are different types declared in that module, so both `Order` and `OrderLine` can have a `total`; a call picks the one whose first parameter matches.
Arguments are passed by position: `shipping(2.5, false)`. Only records and cases are built with named fields. A function with no parameters is called with empty parentheses: `defaults()`.

Functions may call themselves and each other. A call in tail position, the last thing a function does, takes the caller's place on the stack instead of adding to it, so a recursive loop can run as long as it needs to:

`x.f(a, b)` calls `f(x, a, b)`, and `x.f`, with no other arguments, calls `f(x)`: write `x.f`, not `x.f()`. Mo looks for `f` first in the module that declares the type of `x`, then among the names in scope. Chains read left to right: `text.trim.lines.size`.

Where a record's field and a function share a name, `x.name` is the field where the field is visible, and the function elsewhere (section 10.2). When the field holds a function, `x.name(a)` calls it with `a`.

`T.to_text(x)` is `x.to_text`, and `T.compare(a, b)` is `a.compare(b)`, for any type with `Text` or `Order` (section 9.2), including one that has it automatically. `T` is the type, as in `Text.compare(a, b)` or `Option.to_text(found)`, a type parameter, or the module that declares the type: `Shapes.to_text(shape)` takes any type `Shapes` declares. Without arguments they are function values, as in `shapes.map(Shape.to_text)`.
A single capital letter in a signature is a type parameter, and `where` asks for abilities (section 9):

A generic function can't call itself, directly or through other functions, with a type parameter standing for a bigger type built from that parameter. If `depth(t: Tree(T))` leads to a call of `depth` on a `Tree(List(T))`, `T` stands for `List(T)` there, and that is an error. Calling `depth` on a node's `left`, another `Tree(T)`, is fine. Each type a generic function is used with gets its own copy of the function, and such a call would need copies without end: for `Tree(List(T))`, `Tree(List(List(T)))`, and so on.
When a generic function's type parameters aren't decided by its arguments, supply them in brackets before the call, in alphabetical order: `Json.decode[User](text)` or `Json.schema[User]()`.

A named function is a value: `prices.map(with_tax)`. An anonymous function is written `fn(x) ... end`, on one line or several, and its parameter types are inferred. A function type is written like a signature: `fn(Decimal) : Decimal`, or `fn(Text)` for one that returns `Unit`.

An anonymous function can read names in scope where it is made and can declare and assign its own local `var` bindings, but it can't assign a `var` from an enclosing function and can't capture a capability (section 11.4), so it can do only what its parameters allow; it may take a capability as a parameter. So printing each item works in a `for` loop, not inside `map`.

An anonymous function may read a `var` from the function around it only if nothing assigns that `var` after the anonymous function is made, including in a later round of a loop around it. Reading any other `var` is an error, since it would be unclear whether the function sees the value it was made with or a later one. Copy the value into a name first, and read the name:
To use a later value, make the function after the last assignment, or pass the value as a parameter.
`return` and `try` inside an anonymous function leave that anonymous function, not the function around it.

`name = value` binds a name once. A name is visible from its binding to the end of its block: a function's or a test's body, a branch of an `if`, an arm of a `case`, a loop's body, or an anonymous function's body.

Within a function or a test a name means one thing. While a local name, a parameter or a bound name, is visible it can't be bound again, even in an inner block or an anonymous function's parameters. So `line = line.trim` is an error: write `trimmed = line.trim`, or use a `var`. Separate blocks, such as two arms of a `case`, may use the same name. A function also can't refer to one of its module's functions or constants by a name it uses for a local: `fn open(owner: Text)` is fine in a module with an `owner` function, as long as `open` doesn't call `owner(...)`.

Unused names, parameters and imports are errors, and so is a result that isn't `Unit` and isn't used. A name starting with `_` is unused on purpose, `_ = value` discards a non-`Result` value (an unhandled `Result` is still an error, section 8.3), and `for _ in 0..3` repeats without a name.

`var name = value` declares a name that can be assigned again within the function or anonymous function that declares it. Assigning to a field, or to a field of a field, builds a new record with that field changed:

`+=` and `-=` add to and subtract from a `var` or its fields; `mo format` writes `x = x + y` as `x += y`. Assignment never changes a value anyone else holds: whoever holds the old cart still sees the old cart. When the `var` is its value's only holder, the new value reuses its memory.
No parameter is passed by reference: a function returns a new value, and its caller assigns it.

`if` runs a block when its condition is true, with optional `else if` and `else` blocks. With an `else`, an `if` has a value: the value of the block that ran. A block `if` stands on a line of its own or after `=`.
A value that fits on one line uses the one-line form, which always has an `else` and may chain:

`case` compares a value with patterns, top to bottom, and runs the first arm that matches. An arm is `Pattern: statement` on one line, or `Pattern:` followed by lines that run until the next arm or `end`. The value of a `case` is the value of the arm that ran.

The arms must cover every possible value; if they don't, the error lists what's missing. When the value is a choice type, a whole arm can't be a catch-all, `_` or a name: list the cases, so that a case added later shows every place that must handle it. Inside a pattern, `_` and names may stand for anything, as in `Error(_)`. Arms with the same body share a line, as in `Saturday | Sunday: "weekend"`, and an arm may have a guard, as in `Some(n) if n > 10: "many"`.
| `_` | anything, and ignores it |
| `name` | anything, and binds it to `name` |
| `42`, `-1`, `2.5`, `"GET"`, `'x'`, `true` | that literal value |
| `None`, `Some(p)`, `Circle(p)` | that case, with its value matching `p` |
| `Rectangle(width: p, height: q)` | that case or record, with the named fields matching; fields not named are ignored |
| `(p, q)` | a tuple |
| `[]`, `[p, q]`, `[first, ..rest]`, `[first, .._]` | an empty list, a list of exactly two, and a list of at least one, with or without a name for the rest |

A case with named fields is matched by naming them, even when it has only one: `NotFound(path: p)`, or `NotFound(path: _)` to ignore the path. The form `Circle(p)` is only for a case's one unnamed value.

`value is Pattern` tests a pattern, giving a `Bool`. The names the pattern binds are visible where the test is known to be true: in the block of the `if` or `while` it guards, after `and` in the same condition, after `implies`, and after an `assert`.

`for` runs a block for each element of a list, set, map or range, and `while` runs a block while a condition is true. `break` leaves the loop, and `continue` starts its next round. A range `a..b` counts from `a` up to, but not including, `b`.
Mo has no null and no exceptions. A value that may be missing is an `Option`; a function that can fail returns a `Result`; and a bug stops the program (section 13.2). Both are ordinary choice types:

`x or default` gives the value inside a `Some`, or the default for `None`, and computes `default` only for `None`. `x.or_fail(e)` turns `None` into `Error(e)`; it is a function, so `e` is computed even when `x` is a `Some`. `case` and `is` handle both cases:
A function that can fail declares its failures as a choice type, and returns a `Result`:

`try expr` takes the value out of an `Ok`, or returns the `Error` from the function it is in. It works on a `Result` in a function that returns a `Result`, and on an `Option` in a function that returns an `Option`. In a function that returns neither, such as `main : Int` or a test, handle the failure with `case`. When the failure types differ, `try` wraps the failure if the function's failure type has exactly one case that holds it as its unnamed value, as `BadQuantity(QuantityError)` does:
With no such case, or more than one, `try` is an error that says which case to add. Ignoring a `Result` is an error too: every failure is passed upward or handled.
There is no "unwrap". Where a failure truly can't happen, the code says why, with `stop`:

Reaching a `stop` is a bug: the program stops and reports the reason. The reason is fixed text, and `#{...}` in it is an error. A `stop` fits wherever a value is expected, because control never comes back from it. So does a block or arm that ends in `return`: it leaves the function instead of giving a value.
`List(T)`, `Map(K, V)` and your own types take type parameters:

A generic type can't hold itself at a bigger type built from its parameter, as a `Tree(T)` with a field `children: List(Tree(List(T)))` would. Each type a generic type is used with becomes a type of its own, and that one would need types without end, as such a call would for a generic function (section 5.5). `children: List(Tree(T))` is fine.
An ability is something a type can do. There are six, all built in:
| `Equal` | `==` and `!=` | nothing: values are equal when their fields are |
| `Hash` | use as a map key or a set member | nothing: always structural |
| `Order` | `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `sort`, `min` and `max` | `fn compare(a: T, b: T) : Ordering` |
| `Text` | a text form, for `#{...}` and printing | `fn to_text(x: T) : Text` |
| `Number` | `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%` and `sum` | nothing: only `Int`, `BigInt`, `Decimal` and `Float` have it; times and durations also add and subtract (3.9) |

A type with `Hash` or `Order` also has `Equal`. Ability names appear only after `where`, so they don't clash with other names. Records and choice types get `Equal`, `Hash`, `Order` and `Text` automatically whenever all their fields have them. Equality compares field by field; maps compare their entries, and sets their elements, in any order. Order compares fields in the order they are declared, and cases in the order they are declared. Functions and capabilities have no abilities. The built-in types have these:
| `Bool` | yes | yes | `false` first | yes | no |
| `Int`, `BigInt`, `Decimal` | yes | yes | yes | yes | yes |
| `Byte` | yes | yes | yes | yes | no |
| `Float` | IEEE: "not a number" equals nothing | no | yes, with "not a number" last | yes | yes |
| `Text`, `Char` | yes | yes | by character code | yes | no |
| `Bytes` | yes | yes | byte by byte | no | no |
| `Unit` | yes | yes | yes | yes | no |
| `Time`, `Duration` | yes | yes | yes | yes | no (but they add and subtract, 3.9) |
| `Range` | yes | yes | no | yes: `0..3` | no |
| tuples | when every part has it | same | same, part by part from the left | same | no |
| `List(T)` | when `T` has it | same | same, element by element; a list comes before any longer list that begins with it: `[1, 2] < [1, 2, 0]` | same | no |
| `Map(K, V)`, `Set(T)` | when their keys and values have it, comparing entries in any order | same | no | same | no |

`Option`, `Result` and `Ordering` are choice types, so their cases are ordered as they are declared: `None`, `Some`; `Ok`, `Error`; `Less`, `Equal`, `Greater`. `Float` follows IEEE rules: "not a number" equals nothing and sorts last, and floats have no `Hash`, so they can't be map keys.

A value's text form looks like the code that builds it: `Point(x: 1.5, y: 2)`, `Some(3)`, `[1, 2]`, `{"a": 1}`, `(1, true)`, `[1, 2].to_set`. A `Text` or `Char` value's text form is itself; inside another value's, it is quoted and escaped as in code. Numbers have their shortest spelling. A `Float` is written in plain digits, as `1000` or `0.25`, unless its size is below 1e-6 or at least 1e21, when it has an exponent, as `1e21` or `1.5e-7`. A whole float has no `.0`, zero is `0` and negative zero `-0`, and a float that is not a number is `nan`, the infinities `inf` and `-inf`. A `Bool` is `true` or `false`, a `Time` is RFC 3339 text, and a `Duration` is in seconds, as `1.5s`. `x.to_text` gives the text form of any value whose type has `Text`: the same text as `"#{x}"`.
`x.compare(y)` compares two values whose type has `Order`, giving `Less`, `Equal` or `Greater`.
A type customizes `Order` or `Text` with one ordinary function in its own module, which applies wherever the type goes, exposed or not:
There are no user-defined abilities in v0.1. Code that needs something other than these six takes a function as a parameter.

`Json` (with `use Json`) gives `x.to_json : Json`, `Json.encode(x)`, `Json.encode_pretty(x)`, `Json.decode[T](input)` and `Json.decode_strict[T](input)` (where `input` is `Text` or `Bytes`), `Json.from_json[T](json)`, `Json.from_json_strict[T](json)` and `Json.schema[T]()`. `Bool`, `Int`, `Byte`, `Float`, `Text`, `Char`, `Decimal`, `BigInt`, `Time`, `Unit`, `Json` and `JsonNumber` have `Json`; `Decimal` and `BigInt` encode as exact JSON strings, `Time` as RFC 3339 text, `Byte` as `0` to `255`, and `Unit` as `null`. `Bytes`, `Range`, `Duration`, functions, capabilities and maps whose keys aren't `Text` don't have `Json`. Tuples, `List(T)`, `Set(T)`, `Map(Text, V)`, `Option(T)` (`None` is `null`), records and choice types have `Json` whenever all their parts do and no two cases of a choice share a `snake_case` JSON tag.

A record's JSON form is an object of its fields; a missing field of type `Option(T)` decodes as `None`, `decode` and `from_json` ignore unknown object fields, and `decode_strict` and `from_json_strict` reject an unknown field with `Mismatch(path: path, message: message)` naming the dotted path. A choice case with no fields is its `snake_case` string (`InProgress` is `"in_progress"`), a case with one unnamed value is `{"case_name": value}`, and a case with named fields is `{"case_name": {...}}`. A type customizes `Json` in its own module with `fn to_json(x: T) : Json` and `fn from_json(value: Json) : Result(T, Text)`.
A module starts with its name, then the `expose` line listing its public names, then its `use` lines:
Everything not on the `expose` line is private to the module. Tests in the same file see everything (section 12.3).

`expose Order` exposes the type without its fields or cases. Outside the module an `Order` can't be built, taken apart or have its fields read; it can only be passed to the module's functions. `expose OrderError(..)` exposes the fields or cases too. Hidden insides keep values valid: if `place` is the only way to get an `Order`, every `Order` has passed `place`'s checks.

`use Shop.Catalog` lets this module write `Catalog.find(...)` and `Catalog.Item`. `use Shop.Money{Money, add}` also brings those names in unqualified, and a choice type's exposed cases come with it. A module may declare a type with its own name, as the module `Account` declares `Account`: `Account.open(...)` calls the module's function, and `Account` in a type is the type. There are no wildcards and no aliases. A clash between names is an error that suggests the qualified form, and so is a cycle of modules that use each other. The library's `Command`, `Crypto`, `Date`, `Http`, `Json` and `Unicode16` modules are used the same way. Every library module reserves its name, so a program can't declare a module named `Command`, `Crypto`, `Date`, `FileError`, `Files`, `Http`, `Json`, `List`, `Map`, `Option`, `ReadFiles`, `Result`, `Set`, `Text`, `Time` or `Unicode16`. The built-in `Simulation` and `Sqlite` modules also reserve their names. When a `mo.toml` manifest sits in the entry module's folder or an ancestor folder (with `[package]` `name = "..."` and optional `[dependencies]` entries `pkg = { path = "../dir" }` with optional `src = "..."`), `use` resolves a module first under the importing package's root, then across declared path dependencies (`<dir>/src`, `<dir>/lib` and `<dir>`, rejecting malformed manifests, missing folders, dependency cycles or ambiguous duplicate modules with E1110), and finally in the built-in library.
A module may bind fixed values at its top level:

A constant's type comes from its value, which must decide it; for anything else, such as a list of anonymous functions, write a function with a signature. Constants are computed once, before any other code of the program runs, in the order of their dependencies. A constant depends on the constants it uses, directly or through the functions it calls. So a constant may use one written below it, or one in another module, but constants that depend on each other in a cycle are an error. A constant that stops stops the program before it starts. Module-level bindings are constants, not mutable state. A service declares its state separately (section 11.5); handlers receive that state as an argument and return any replacement state.

Always in scope: the built-in types of section 3, `Option` with `Some` and `None`, `Result` with `Ok` and `Error`, `Ordering` with its cases, the capability types, `FileError` with its cases, `SimulationError` with `ServiceDown` and `ToolFailed`, `Entry` with `EntryKind` and its cases, `NetworkError`, and `SqliteError`. The cases of `NetworkError` and `SqliteError` are not in scope by themselves: they are written with `Network.` or `Sqlite.` in front, as in `Network.TimedOut` and `Sqlite.OutsideFolder` (section 14). The functions of section 14 belong to their types' modules: call them with a dot, as in `text.lines`, or through the module, as in `Set.empty` and `Time.parse(text)`. So a local may be called `lines` or `count` without clashing with them.

A function can affect or observe the world outside the program only through capabilities it is handed as parameters. A capability's type names what it can do: `Console` prints, `Files` reads and writes files, `Clock` tells the time. So a function's parameter types are its complete list of effects, and a function with no parameter that is or holds a capability only computes: given the same arguments, it always gives the same result.
| `Args` | read its command-line arguments |
| `Env` | read environment variables |
| `Console` | print to standard output and standard error, and read standard input |
| `Files` | read and write files in one folder and the folders inside it |
| `ReadFiles` | only read them |
| `Clock` | read the current time and sleep |
| `Random` | draw random numbers |
| `Network` | open connections to other computers |
| `Connection` | send and receive bytes on one open connection |
| `Sqlite` | open and query SQLite databases in the program's folder |
| `Sqlite.Database` | run SQL statements and queries on one open database |
| `Command` | run confined external programs inside one folder (with `use Command`) |
| `SecureRandom` | draw cryptographically secure random bytes |
| `Files.File` | read, write, resize, sync and lock bytes at arbitrary offsets on one open file |

`main` lists the capabilities the program needs, in any order and at most one of each type. The runtime hands over exactly those, so a program's whole authority is on its first line. The `Files`, `ReadFiles`, `Sqlite` or `Command` it gets reach the folder the program was started in. `main` can't list a `Connection`, a `Sqlite.Database` or a `Files.File`: a program gets them only from a `Network`, a `Sqlite`, a `Files` or a `ReadFiles`.

`main` returns nothing, and the program exits with status 0; or an `Int`, the exit status, from 0 to 255; or `Result(Unit, E)`, where `Error(e)` prints `e`'s text form to standard error and exits with status 1.

A capability can be narrowed before it is passed on. `files.within("reports")` reaches only that folder, `files.read_only` returns a `ReadFiles`, which can only read, `network.allow_hosts(["api.example.com:443"])` returns a `Network` that opens connections only to the listed destinations, and `command.within("work").allow_programs(["mo", "git"])` narrows a `Command` to that folder and those program basenames (section 14). Calling `within` with a path that would leave the folder, such as `".."`, gives a capability that reaches nothing (section 14). Pass each function the least it needs:
- Records may hold capabilities, so a function that needs several can take one record.
- Anonymous functions can't capture capabilities, or values holding them. A function that needs one takes it as a parameter.
- Only the runtime makes real capabilities. Tests, examples and promises use fakes (section 12.4).
- Capabilities have no abilities: they can't be compared, printed or used as keys.
- There are no log statements. To report something, print it or return it.
This build checks service blocks. `mo run` of a service entry module still reports E1408; see the end of this section.

A module may declare one top-level `service ... end` block. Its clauses name the state type and start value, local functions offered as tools, timer handlers, the environment variable holding its access token, and the promises the service keeps (section 12.2). `service` is reserved. The clause words `state`, `tools`, `every`, `token`, `from`, `env` and `on` remain ordinary identifiers outside their clause positions.

Clauses occur in this order: exactly one `state`, exactly one `tools` naming at least one function, zero or more `every` clauses, exactly one `token`, then zero or more service promises. Empty services and timer-only services are refused. No function name may appear twice anywhere in the block, including across tools and timers.

The start value has the declared state type. The runtime uses it only when there is no saved state. Each tool is a function declared in this module whose first two parameters are the state type and `Time`, the moment the message arrived. The service selects the local overload whose first parameter exactly matches its state type, then requires that signature to contain no unresolved generic parameters. Generic helpers can be called through concrete wrappers. A service block has no explicit generic-specialization syntax. The state, handler inputs and handler results must contain neither capabilities nor function values, including inside records, choices, tuples and collections.

Tool names cannot end in `?` (E0106). Arguments after State and Time, the reply and any application error must have visible fields and cases, including nested types (E0105). Imported wire types need their representation exposed with `(..)`; types declared in this module are visible locally. Private service state need not be exposed. These wire checks run after the bare-state result check E0101.

A tool updates stored state only when it returns `(State, Reply)` or `Result((State, Reply), E)`. Returning exactly `State`, or `Result(State, E)`, is an error. For a bare `State` result, the error offers two fixes: return `(state, Unit)` to update state, or wrap the value in a record to return it as read-only data. `Result(State, E)` receives no fixes. `mo fix` applies neither alternative. The suggested adapters retain the tool's name and `##` comment, rename the original function to a helper, and rebind the module's references to that helper. A function on the module's `expose` line receives no fixes, because a fix can't update callers in other modules. Nor does a function whose name ends in `?`: it must return `Bool` (section 2.3), so neither adapter could keep its name. Every other result shape is a read-only reply, including `List(State)`, `Option(State)` and records containing state. Read-only messages are neither logged nor saved. Logged and saved mean the service's state and its recovery log: a record of a failed call kept for diagnosis (section 13.4) is neither, and keeping one never changes the state, the log or what recovery restores.

Each `every` clause has a duration literal with a whole-number value of at least 1, such as `1.minute` or `30.seconds`, and a local handler with exactly the signature `(State, Time): State`. Simultaneous ticks follow the source order of the `every` clauses. Unlike a tool returning bare state, a timer handler returns replacement state. Handlers remain ordinary functions that examples, promises and tests can call directly.

The token source is a plain text literal naming an environment variable. The name is nonempty and contains only uppercase ASCII letters, digits and `_`, and cannot start with a digit. Checking does not read that variable or run a service. This build checks, tests, formats and fixes service modules, but `mo run` of a service entry module reports E1408, "mo run does not start services yet". Importing a service module does not start it.

`mo serve` (section 13.4) exposes a service through authenticated MCP over plain HTTP/1.1. It provides no new Mo function or capability. A tool's `structuredContent` is an object with `value` on success or `error` on failure; one text-content block contains the same compact object. Runtime errors report an effect of `none`, `applied` or `unknown` on this call's service state. An effect does not promise retry safety; an updating call whose response is lost has an unknown effect from the client's perspective.

A module declares at most one HTTP API server with `api ... end`, and never alongside `service` (E0108). An `api` block has at least one route (`get`, `post`, `put`, `patch` or `delete`, directly or inside `scope "/prefix" ... end` blocks nested up to 8 levels deep) and optional `port` (`0` to `65535`, by default `8000`), `cors` (a nonempty single-line origin or `"*"`), `sqlite name from "path"` (up to 16 relative paths inside `--data` with no `..`), `actor name: ActorType` (up to 16 distinct actor types), `static "/prefix" from "dir"` (up to 8 non-overlapping URL prefixes mapped to confined relative folders inside `--data`, served before route dispatch on `GET` and `HEAD` with MIME types, `ETag`/`If-None-Match` `304`, `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and `Cache-Control`), `auth Principal via handler` (where `Principal` is a concrete `struct` or `enum` and `handler`, a local `fn` or imported `Module.fn`, returns `Result(Principal, Error)`), `job "name" handler` or `job "name" handler every Duration` clauses (up to 16 distinct whitespace-free job names with positive integer `.second(s)`, `.minute(s)`, `.hour(s)` or `.day(s)` intervals), and `status` clauses (E0108).

Each route names an HTTP method, a plain text path template (`""` inside a `scope` or starting with `/`), and a non-generic, non-overloaded local `fn` or imported `Module.fn`, with distinct `(method, shape)` pairs across the block after concatenating enclosing `scope` prefixes and normalizing `:param` segments (E0109). Route parameters bind by type and name in any order: `Principal` (running `auth` before the handler and short-circuiting on `Error`), `Option(Principal)` (running `auth` and passing `Some(m)` on `Ok(m)` or `None` on `Error(_)`), `Api.Request`, `Sqlite.Database` (matching a `sqlite` clause by parameter name, ignoring a leading `_`), an actor handle (matching an `actor` clause by parameter name and type, ignoring a leading `_`), a capability (`Sqlite`, `Network`, `Command`, `Clock`, `Random`, `SecureRandom`, `Files`, `ReadFiles`, `Env` or `Console`), a `:param` scalar (`Int`, `Byte`, `BigInt`, `Decimal`, `Bool` or `Text`), an `Option` scalar query parameter, a required scalar query parameter on `get` or `delete`, or at most one `Json` request body parameter on `post`, `put` or `patch` decoded strictly with `Json.from_json_strict` so invalid path segments, missing or malformed query parameters, malformed JSON and unknown fields answer status `422` without calling the handler (E0109). Each `job` handler is a non-generic, non-overloaded local `fn` or imported `Module.fn` taking `payload: Json` first followed by any declared `Sqlite.Database`, `actor` or capability parameters in any order and returning `Unit` or `Result(Unit, E)` where `E` has `Text` (E0108).

A route returns `Api.Response`, `Unit` (status `204`), a `Json` value (status `200`), or `Result` of one of those and either `Api.Response` or a concrete error `enum` whose cases are visible and have `Json`. Every case of every error `enum` returned by `auth` or any route is mapped once to a status code from `100` to `599` with `status Case = code`, or `status Case(_) = code` when the case carries fields, and a response encodes the error with `to_json` at that status (E0110). Every `api` also serves OpenAPI 3.1.0 JSON at `GET /openapi.json` (with route summaries from `##` comments, `bearerAuth` on authenticated routes, parameter and body schemas from `Json.schema`, and mapped error status codes), an interactive HTML page at `GET /docs`, `204` CORS preflight on `OPTIONS` when `cors` is set, `405` when a path matches another method, and `404` otherwise.

A module declares at most one in-process stateful actor capability with `actor Name ... end`, and never alongside `service` (E0111, E0099). Its clauses occur in order: `state Type = expr`, `calls fn1, fn2, ...` naming at least one local handler, zero or more `every Duration fn` timers, and zero or more `promise` or `promise on call` invariants (section 12.2); an `actor` has no `token` clause (E0111). `actor` and `Actor` are reserved, while `calls` remains an ordinary identifier outside its clause position.

`Name` is an opaque capability type (without abilities and never exposed with `(..)`): it can be listed once per actor type on `main` (section 11.2), bound with `actor name: Name` in an `api` block (section 11.6), passed as a function parameter, or started deterministically in tests with `Actor.start(Name)` or `Actor.start_at(Name, at)` (section 12.4). Actor state, call inputs and replies follow `service`'s purity, visibility and update rules (section 11.5): a handler takes `(State, Time, ...)` and returns `Reply` (read-only), `(State, Reply)` (updating), or `Result((State, Reply), E)` (updating on `Ok`).

Calling `handle.call(args...)` (or `handle.call` with no extra arguments) sends a synchronous message into the actor's isolated heap and projects the state out, returning `Reply` or `Result(Reply, E)` and stopping the caller if the actor is stopped or the handler fails with a bug; `Actor.send(handle, Name.call, args...)` returns `Result(ProjectedReply, SimulationError)` instead. In `mo serve` and `mo run`, each declared actor runs in memory with serialized mailbox access, timers and supervisor restarts (5 failures in 60 seconds restart from its initial state, and 3 restarts in 10 minutes stop it); `mo test` runs `Module.service.recovery` and `Module.service.promise.N` on every actor.
A function's specification sits at the top of its body: its promises and examples, then a blank line, then its code. Leaving out the blank line is not an error; `mo format` writes it.
`examples` lists calls with their expected results. Each line is a `Bool` expression, usually `call == expected`, and `mo test` checks every line:
A `promise` states what must hold for every call. It has a body, an optional label, and optional anchors:
- **an optional label**: a plain text literal after `promise` naming what is promised, when a short label helps;
- **a body**: one or more `Bool` lines over the parameters and `result`, the function's result, which must all be true;
- **optional anchors**: `allows` and `forbids` lines. Each gives every parameter and `result` a value, which the body must accept (`allows`) or reject (`forbids`).

When anchors are written, the compiler checks that the body accepts every `allows` and rejects every `forbids`. `mo test` checks the body against the function on many generated inputs, boundaries first, and fails any vacuous condition: a condition that is always true, or an `a implies b` condition whose left side `a` is never true across all `examples` and generated inputs. It builds a type exposed without its insides only through a limited number of calls to its module's exposed functions, other types from any values of their fields, and capabilities as fakes. A value built that way can come with another such value that the same call returned, so a `Lease` can arrive with the `Queue` that issued it. A promise speaks about calls that return; a call that stops on a generated input is reported as a bug, with the input. The boundaries include each type's extremes, such as `Decimal`'s largest value and the last instant of the year 9999, so a promise that passes holds for every call its types allow. When an extreme stops a call, the report says so, as in "stops with overflow when `amount` is `Decimal`'s largest value", and shows the two fixes: return a failure for such inputs, or take a type whose module keeps its values in range. Proofs come in a later version.

After a false promise, `mo test` tries smaller inputs, keeping only those that still fail. For a hidden type, it shortens the recorded builder sequence and simplifies the arguments to those calls; it never edits hidden fields. Values used as same-call companions stay whole. Builder reduction and other input shrinking share at most 200 additional subject calls and the original deadline; the reported counterexample need not be the smallest possible one.

Recording is optional and bounded to 4096 builder recipes per generated tuple, including recipes made during unsuccessful starts. Exhaustion does not change which inputs can be generated or whether they pass. If that tuple fails with incomplete recording, the report keeps the original failing input and adds E1404 explaining that shrinking is limited.

For a generic function, `mo test` checks every concrete instantiation already present in the program, including those supplied by anchors, examples and tests. It keeps each complete list of type arguments as used; it does not combine arguments from different uses or choose additional types. It generates and shrinks values separately for each instance, and a failure names its concrete types. This checks those instances, not every possible substitution for the function's type parameters.

A promise about a whole service is written in its `service` block, after `token`. A step promise holds across every step the service takes: a tool call, a clock advance, or a crash and restart. Its body reads `before`, `after` and `now`. A tool promise, `promise on submit` (or `promise "…" on submit`), holds after every call to that tool that replied, and also reads the tool's arguments by name and `reply`, what the caller received. Any anchors give each of those names a value. `mo test` checks service promises on the recovery check's generated sequences (section 12.5) and reports a failure as a short sequence that still fails.

For a crash and restart, `before` is the state at the crash and `after` the state once recovery and the restart's startup ticks have run. `reply` is `R` for a tool that returns `(State, R)` or a read-only `R`, and `Result(R, E)` for one that returns `Result((State, R), E)`. A tool parameter named `before`, `after`, `now` or `reply`, an `on` that names none of the block's tools, or a service promise outside a `service` block is E0107. A service has at most 64 service promises (E1109).
There are no preconditions. What a caller must guarantee becomes a type, such as a `Quantity` that its module never builds negative, or a failure, such as `Error(InvalidAmount)`.

A `test` names a scenario in a sentence and checks it with `assert`. Tests live in the same file as the code and see its private names. A name bound by `assert ... is Pattern` stays in scope for the rest of its block:

Tests, examples and promises make fake capabilities, which reach nothing outside the program: `Console.fake()`, whose `printed` and `printed_errors` list the lines written to standard output and standard error; `Console.fake_input(lines)`, which also has those lines to read; `Files.in_memory(files)`, from a map of paths to texts; `Clock.fixed(time)`; `Random.seeded(n)`; `SecureRandom.seeded(n)`; `Args.of(list)`; `Env.of(map)`; `Network.fake(peers)`, from a map of the requests it answers (section 14); `Sqlite.fake()` and `Sqlite.in_memory()`, an in-memory SQLite capability (section 14); `Command.fake(replies)`, from a map of encoded command exchanges (section 14); `Simulation.start(module, at)` for a test service; and `ApiTest.start(Module, ...)` (returning a reusable `ApiTest.App` handle), `ApiTest.send(Module, request, ...)` or `ApiTest.run_job(Module, name, payload, ...)` to dispatch an `Api.Request` or a declared background job directly against `Module`'s `api` block in memory with optional fake capabilities (synthesizing empty fakes for any capabilities omitted). Fakes are made only there, never in a module's constants or its functions. `printed` and `printed_errors` can be used only there too, where every console is a fake, and using them anywhere else is an error.

`Simulation.start(Module, at: Time) : Simulation` starts the selected service with an in-memory store and runs its startup ticks. `Simulation.send(handle, Module.tool, args...)` supplies state and the current fake time, then returns `Result(R, SimulationError)` for the tool's complete declared result R. Only direct module and registered tool selectors are allowed, including registered tools not listed in `expose`. Timers, other private functions and function values are not selectors. Arguments after the selector exactly match the tool's parameters after State and Time. An application `Error(e)` is returned as `Ok(Error(e))`; it does not count toward the failure limit. `ServiceDown` means nothing was queued, and `ToolFailed` means a handler defect or work/memory limit, with no update committed. A state-changing `Ok(r)` means committed. Each `ToolFailed` counts toward the service's failure limit: 5 within 60 seconds of simulated time restart the service from its last saved state, and 3 such restarts within 10 minutes stop it, after which `send` returns `ServiceDown` until `restart`. Call these operations through the module, as in `Simulation.crash(sim)`; dot calls such as `sim.crash` are not available.

`Simulation.advance(handle, by: Duration)`, `Simulation.crash(handle)` and `Simulation.restart(handle)` return Unit. Advance visits each deadline in order, supplies that deadline as `now`, and drains simultaneous timers in service source order. Zero does nothing. A crashed service's clock advances without running handlers. Before advancing a running service, all due firings are counted separately; more than 10,000 is a bug with no clock movement, execution or commit. Negative advances and times beyond year 9999 are bugs. Each successful operation returns with an empty mailbox. Send is synchronous and cannot be interrupted by crash.

Crash is idempotent. It discards live state, timers and supervisor history, but retains the same open store and clock. Restart recovers through the real log and snapshots, emits no replies for replay, and starts fresh supervision and startup ticks. Restarting a running service or selecting another service's tool is a bug. Copies of the capability share its identity; its last release closes the service and then the store. Helpers holding the handle may use all operations except start. Like other capabilities, Simulation cannot be stored in service state or tool signatures, and cannot be a main parameter.

Startup, timer, persistence and invalid-recovery failures stop the test with a bug report, not a SimulationError. Arguments and replies are copied into and out of the service, limited to 128 levels of nesting, 1,048,576 values and 16 MiB encoded, including read-only and application Error replies. Copy-in failure queues and commits nothing. Updating messages also obey the aggregate saved-message byte limit; an admission refusal reports that no handler ran and does not count toward the failure limit. Read-only messages are not saved. Copy-out failure names the executed tool and any committed update; it does not roll back or retry. A promise whose inputs include a `Simulation` is E1400: `mo test` generates steps against a service only in its recovery check (section 12.5), which also checks the promises written in its `service` block (section 12.2).

A capability is a handle on something outside the program, and a fake is a handle on something kept for the test. Every use of one fake sees the same files and the same output: a file that `main` writes to a `Files.in_memory(...)` fake can be read back, and a `Console.fake()` passed to `main` shows afterwards what `main` printed.

`mo test` checks that every service in the program recovers what it committed. Each service gets one recovery check, named after its module, as in `Counter.service.recovery`; its author writes nothing for it.

The check runs the service on an in-memory store, as `Simulation` does, through generated sequences of steps. A step calls a tool, advances the clock, or crashes the service and then restarts it. Tool arguments are generated from the tool's parameter types, as a promise's inputs are, and often reuse values an earlier reply returned, keeping the values of one reply together, so a sequence can acknowledge the job it leased. Every sequence ends with a crash and a restart. Crashes fall between steps, never inside a commit.

After each restart, the recovered state must equal the state the service held just before the crash. The service commits each update before it replies, so that is the state an uninterrupted run reaches from the same committed updates and timer firings. Equal means the same saved encoding, which is stricter than `==`: a Map or Set keeps its order and a Float its bits. The state is compared before the restart's startup ticks run; timers that fell due while the service was down are not run.

The check fails when a recovered state differs, or when recovery refuses the store. Application errors, `ToolFailed`, failing timer handlers, `ServiceDown` and the supervisor's restarts and stops are ordinary steps; after a stop, the next step is a restart, compared against the state at the stop. When the start value or an interval fails as the service first opens, the check stops with that failure.

The same sequences check the service's promises (section 12.2): after each step every step promise, and after each call that replied every promise on that tool. Each is listed and selected as `Module.service.promise.N`, numbered in source order, just before its service's recovery check, and fails on its own. A promise body runs under the same work limit as a tool call; one that runs past it stops that promise.

Every check is listed and selected like any other (section 13.4). It runs its whole plan: `--calls` sequences, 200 by default, each seeded from the service's name and its number, so every run reports the same result. `--seconds` does not apply. A sequence has at most 64 steps and 8 restarts.

A failing sequence is shrunk: steps are deleted, a crash always with its restart, then arguments are simplified and advances shortened, within 200 additional sequence runs. A shorter sequence is kept only when it fails the same check, and for a promise on the same line. The shrunk sequence runs once more before it is reported, and fails the same way. The report numbers the steps, a crash and its restart counting as two, and gives each tool call's arguments as literal values and each step's outcome. A recovery failure shows the state before the crash beside the state recovery produced; a promise failure marks the step that broke it, shows the states before and after that step, and points at the line that was false.

`mo test FILE --mutants` also judges the checks themselves. A mutant is a copy of the program with one small change to the code of one function, which `mo test` makes on its own. Each change is of one of seven kinds, named in its report:
- `boundary`: a comparison moved to its boundary, `<` and `<=` swapped, and `>` and `>=`;
- `negate`: a comparison negated, `==` and `!=` swapped, `<` made `>=`, `<=` made `>`, `>` made `<=`, and `>=` made `<`;
- `logic`: `and` and `or` swapped;
- `not`: a `not` removed;
- `arithmetic`: `+` and `-` swapped, and `*` and `/`;
- `bool`: a Bool literal flipped;
- `int`: an Int literal raised by one.

Each operator or literal in a function's code gives one mutant. Promises, examples, tests, a service block and code outside a function are never changed. The functions changed are those of the file given and of the program modules it imports; a library module's functions are changed only when `mo test` is given that module. A mutant the checker refuses, such as `name or "world"` made `name and "world"`, is dropped.

A mutant is killed when a check that passed on the program does not pass on it: the check fails, stops with a bug, has an anchor fail, or takes more than four times the steps it took on the program and more than 1,000,000. It is also killed when the program no longer starts. Any check can kill a mutant: a promise, an example, a test or a recovery check. A mutant runs only against the checks that ran its function, cheapest first, and stops at the first that kills it. A mutant that no check kills survives, and is an error, E1439, that names the function, the line and the change; when no check runs that function at all, the error says so.
Killing every mutant is a floor on how thoroughly a program's checks run its code. It is not evidence that the checks catch the mistakes a person or agent would make.

Mo evaluates eagerly, left to right: a call's arguments, then the call; an operator's left side, then its right. `and`, `or` and `implies` skip their right side when the left decides the answer, and `x or default` on an `Option` computes `default` only when `x` is `None`. `try` returns early, and `stop` stops the program.

A bug stops the program at once, with a report of what happened and where, and exit status 70. These are bugs: overflow in `Int`, `Decimal` or `Duration` arithmetic, or a time outside the years 1 to 9999; dividing by zero; reaching a `stop`; using more stack, call depth or memory than section 13.4's limits allow, or more memory than the machine has; calling a library function outside what it accepts, such as `take(-1)` or `random.int(5, 5)`; two keys of a map literal that turn out equal (section 3.8); an exit status outside 0 to 255; printing to an output that is gone; having too many folders or too many connections open at once; and a fake whose files make one path both a file and a folder (section 14). Bugs are never caught.
Mo promises what operations cost, not how values are stored:
| `get`, `size`, `first` and `last` on a list | constant |
| `append` on a list, and assigning a `var`'s field | constant when the value has one holder; a copy when it's shared |
| `get` on a map, and `has?` on a map or a set | constant on average |
| `set` and `remove` on a map, and `add` and `remove` on a set | constant on average when the value has one holder; a copy when it's shared |
| `byte_count` | constant |
| `char_count`, `split`, `lines`, `contains?` | proportional to the text's length |
| `sort`, `sort_by` and `sort_by_desc` | n log n, and stable: equal keys keep their order |
A value is shared when two names, fields or collections hold it. Changing a value with one holder reuses its memory; changing a shared value copies it first, and its other holders keep the old value.

Each command is given the file of the program's main module; `mo check` and `mo test` also accept a library module. `mo check FILE` reports the program's errors, `mo run [--root DIR] [--state-dir DIR] FILE [ARGS...]` runs it with the arguments after the file's name (granting `DIR`, `.` by default, as the starting folder for `Files`, `ReadFiles` and `Command`, and for `Sqlite` unless `--state-dir` names another folder), and `mo test FILE` checks its examples, promises and tests. `mo diff [OLD] NEW` compares `NEW` against `OLD`, or against Git `HEAD` when `OLD` is omitted: it reports authority changes (capability parameters and literal `within`, `read_only`, `allow_hosts` and `allow_programs` narrowings), exposed signature, `api` route and `cors`, and service tool changes, state schema changes, and runs `OLD`'s promises, service promises and examples against `NEW`, exiting 1 when authority expands or a contract fails or stops. `mo emit FILE -o OUT` checks the program as `mo check` does and writes its bytecode to `OUT`; `-o` is required, and a library module has no main to emit (E0079). `mo install FILE [--name NAME] [--bin-dir DIR] [--root DIR] [--state-dir DIR]` compiles a main program to verified bytecode and installs an executable launcher in `DIR` (`~/.local/bin` by default). `mo serve FILE --port N --data DIR [--allow-host NAME] [--admin-socket PATH] [--ready-file PATH]` runs the service `FILE` declares (section 11.5) over MCP on 127.0.0.1, with its saved state in the folder `DIR`, which must exist; `--allow-host` also accepts requests that give `NAME` as their host, as a proxy in front of it does, and `mo serve FILE [--port N] [--bind HOST] [--workers N] [--watch] [--data DIR] [--ready-file PATH]` runs an `api` server `FILE` declares (section 11.6) over concurrent HTTP/1.1 keep-alive (defaulting to `127.0.0.1`, `8` workers from `1` to `64`, the `api` block's `port` or an ephemeral OS port when `--port 0` is given, and `.` for `--data`; `--ready-file PATH` atomically writes JSON with `url`, `port`, `pid`, `data_dir` and `started_at` once the listener is bound and ready), logging sanitized request lines, pooling per-worker SQLite connections with automatic rollback on defect, running declared `api` background jobs (periodic `every` ticks and durable `arvo_jobs` queue rows with exponential-backoff retry and stale-lock recovery) in isolated processes, reloading changed `.mo` modules and `mo.toml` path dependencies under `--watch`, and isolating each request so a handler bug logs a failure and answers status `500` without stopping the server. Public HTTP on a service exposes only the service's declared tools. When `--admin-socket PATH` is given, `mo serve` binds a mode-0600 Unix domain socket at `PATH` exposing built-in operator views and live `mo push` upgrade tools, authenticated by OS filesystem permissions. `mo fetch --admin-socket PATH --export state|failure ID --out FILE`, run on the same host, saves an export of the state or of one retained failure over the admin socket to a new private file. `mo format` and `mo fix` rewrite the files they are given, and `mo format --stdin` formats standard input to standard output. `mo guide` needs no file. It prints a short guide for agents writing Mo, matched to the installed version: how to work with the `mo` command, a small complete program with its tests, and when a task is done. `mo guide --reference` prints this reference. `mo` exits with status 0 when everything passed, 1 when the program has errors or an example, promise, test or recovery check fails, and 2 for a mistake in the command itself. Once the program runs, `mo run` exits with the program's own status (section 11.2), or 70 after a bug (section 13.2). `mo serve` exits with 0 after SIGTERM or SIGINT, 1 when it cannot start the service, 69 when repeated failures stop the service, 75 when another process holds its saved state for longer than the 10 seconds it waits, and 70 when it dies any other way.

`mo test` runs every example, promise, test and recovery check unless it's told which. Each has a full name: its function's name, or a test's module's, then its kind and a number counted from 1 in source order, such as `Wc.count.example.3` for the third example of `Wc.count`, `Account.transfer.promise.1`, or `Wc.test.2` for the second test in `Wc`. A recovery check's full name is its service module's, then `service.recovery`, and a service promise's its service module's, then `service.promise` and its number (section 12.5). `--only NAME` runs the one with that full name, and can be given more than once; `--in MODULE` runs one module's, still checking the whole program; and `--list` prints the full names without running anything. `--strength DIR` measures how many of the wrong versions in `DIR` the program's promises and examples kill, and how many any of its checks kills; it takes no `--only`, `--in`, `--list` or `--calls`. `--jobs N` (`1` to `256`, by default the host's available cores; `--jobs 1` runs serially) parallelizes `--mutants` and `--strength` across worker threads while preserving deterministic output order. A selection that matches nothing is a mistake in the command.

Each promise runs up to `--calls` generated inputs, 200 by default, and stops after `--seconds`, 2 by default, passing on the inputs it reached; each service check runs all of its `--calls` sequences (section 12.5). `mo test FILE --mutants` runs every check with no time limit, then tries every mutant (section 12.6) if all checks pass, and before the totals counts the mutants tried, those killed by each kind of check and by the program no longer starting, those that survived and those dropped. `--mutants` takes no `--only`, `--in`, `--calls`, `--seconds`, `--max` limit, `--bundle` or `--strength`. `--list` lists the selected checks without running anything, and with `--mutants` also lists each mutant `--mutants` would try and how many mutants each function has.

`mo run` and `mo test` limit what a program uses: `--max-stack` sets the bytes of stack, by default 8 MiB; `--max-depth` the calls in progress at once, by default 10,000; and `--max-heap` the bytes of memory, by default 1 GiB. Going past one is a bug whose report names the limit (section 13.2). A call in tail position takes its caller's place on the stack and doesn't count toward the depth (section 5.3). A program can't set its own limits.

`mo history DIR` shows what a stopped service's data folder holds, without starting the service or running any of its code: the last snapshot of its state and the sequence it was taken at, the messages logged after it by sequence, handler, arrival time and argument sizes, and each retained failure record with the build that recorded it. It never waits for the folder and refuses one a running service owns; `--recover` lets it first roll back a write that a stopped service left unfinished. `mo replay FILE --failure ID (--data DIR | --export ARTIFACT)` runs a retained failure's handler again on the state, arrival time and arguments it recorded, and reports whether the same failure was `reproduced`. `FILE` must be the unchanged program that recorded the failure, and the `mo` that replays it the one that recorded it. `--fix REVISED` then runs the handler of the same name in the program `REVISED` on the same inputs, and its verdict is `verified` only when the original failure reproduced and the revision succeeded. `mo query FILE FUNCTION` runs a function of the program over an exported or live state (`--export ARTIFACT` or `--admin-socket PATH`) or over a retained failure's inputs (`--failure ID` with `--data DIR`, `--export ARTIFACT` or `--admin-socket PATH`). The function takes the state type of `FILE`'s service, then for a failure `Time` and the handler's arguments in order, and its parameters and result hold no capability or function. A query takes `mo run`'s limits and `--max-work`, the instructions it may run, by default 1,073,741,824. Each of these commands refuses an input it cannot use before anything runs, naming what differs. They exit 0 when the result they report holds, 1 when it does not or they refuse, and 2 for a mistake in the command; `mo query` exits 70 when its function stops with a bug (section 13.2).

`mo check --json`, `mo test --json`, `mo diff --json`, and `--json` on `mo replay`, `mo query` and `mo history` write one JSON object per line to standard output: first the format's version, then one for each error and for each example, promise and test run or each outcome reported (including `mutant_killed`, `mutant_survived` and `mutant_summary` on `mo test --json --mutants`, and `strength_case` and `strength_summary` on `mo test --json --strength DIR`), and last the totals and the exit status. Within a major version of the format, every field keeps its name, type and meaning, and an error's code keeps its meaning; new fields and new kinds of object may be added, so a reader skips what it doesn't know. A message's wording may change.

Each function is listed under the type of its first parameter, written as it is called with a dot: under **Text**, `split(separator: Text) : List(Text)` is called as `text.split(",")`. A function written `Type.name(...)` is called through the type's module. `pred` is a function returning a `Bool`. Calling a function outside what it accepts, such as `take(-1)`, is a bug (section 13.2). Every type with the `Text` ability also has `to_text : Text`, its text form, and every type with `Order` has `compare(other: T) : Ordering` (section 9.2).

**Int**: `abs`, `min(b: Int)`, `max(b: Int)`, `pow(n: Int)` (`n` at least 0), `floor_div(b: Int)`, `floor_mod(b: Int)`, and `wrapping_add`, `wrapping_sub`, `wrapping_mul`, `saturating_add`, `saturating_sub` and `saturating_mul` (each taking `b: Int`), all `: Int`. `checked_add`, `checked_sub` and `checked_mul` `(b: Int) : Option(Int)`. `to_decimal : Decimal`, `to_float : Float` (rounded to the nearest float), `to_big : BigInt`, `to_byte : Option(Byte)`, `to_char : Option(Char)`, `to_text : Text`. `seconds`, `milliseconds`, `minutes`, `hours` and `days : Duration`, also named `second`, `millisecond`, `minute`, `hour` and `day` respectively (3.9).

**BigInt**: the arithmetic operators, `abs`, `min(b: BigInt)`, `max(b: BigInt)`, `pow(n: Int)`, `floor_div(b: BigInt)` and `floor_mod(b: BigInt)`, all `: BigInt`; `to_int : Option(Int)`, `to_text : Text`. **Byte**: `to_int : Int`, `to_text : Text`.

**Decimal**: `abs`, `min(b: Decimal)`, `max(b: Decimal)`, `round(places: Int)` (ties away from zero), `floor` and `ceil`, all `: Decimal`. `to_int : Option(Int)` (`None` unless whole and in range), `to_float : Float` (rounded to the nearest float), `to_fixed(places: Int) : Text` (rounded as `round` does), `to_text : Text`. `places` is from 0 to 18.

**Float**: `abs`, `floor`, `ceil`, `round` (ties away from zero) and `sqrt`, all `: Float`; `nan?` and `infinite? : Bool`; `to_decimal : Option(Decimal)`: the number the float's text form writes, rounded to 18 places with ties to even, so `0.1.to_decimal` is `Some(0.1)`, and `None` for not-a-number, the infinities and anything beyond `Decimal`'s range; `to_text : Text`.

**Text**: `byte_count : Int`, `char_count : Int`, `empty? : Bool`, `chars : List(Char)`, `bytes : Bytes`. `lines : List(Text)`: split where `\n` or `\r\n` ends a line, without the line endings; `""` has none, a final line break doesn't start another line, and a `\r` alone stays in its line. `words : List(Text)`: split at ASCII white space, which alone gives none. ASCII white space is space, tab, line feed, vertical tab, form feed and carriage return. `split(separator: Text) : List(Text)`: the separator isn't empty, and empty pieces are kept, so `"".split(",")` is `[""]`. `trim`, `trim_start` and `trim_end : Text` (ASCII white space). `starts_with?(prefix: Text)`, `ends_with?(suffix: Text)` and `contains?(part: Text) : Bool`. `drop_prefix(prefix: Text)` and `drop_suffix(suffix: Text) : Option(Text)`: `None` when the text doesn't have it. `replace(old: Text, new: Text)` (`old` isn't empty), `repeat(n: Int)` (`n` is at least 0), `pad_left(width: Int)` and `pad_right(width: Int)`, all `: Text`; padding adds spaces, counting characters, and leaves text that is already as wide, or wider, unchanged, even for a width below 0. `ascii_lowercase` and `ascii_uppercase : Text`. `to_int : Option(Int)`: an optional `-` and ASCII digits, in the `Int` range, and nothing else. `to_decimal : Option(Decimal)`: an optional `-`, one or more ASCII digits, then optionally `.` and 1 to 18 digits, in the `Decimal` range, and nothing else, so `"1."` and `".5"` give `None`. `to_float : Option(Float)`: an optional `-`, one or more ASCII digits, optionally `.` and one or more digits, and optionally `e` or `E`, an optional sign and one or more digits; or exactly `nan`, `inf` or `-inf`, the text forms of section 9.2. It gives the nearest float, and `None` for anything else or for a number too large to be a finite `Float`. `Text.from_chars(chars: List(Char)) : Text`.
**Char**: `code : Int`, `ascii_digit?`, `ascii_letter?` and `ascii_white_space? : Bool`, `ascii_lowercase` and `ascii_uppercase : Char`, `to_text : Text`.

**Bytes**: `size : Int`, `empty? : Bool`, `get(i: Int) : Option(Byte)`, `decode_utf8 : Option(Text)`. `slice(from: Int, to: Int) : Bytes` gives the bytes from position `from` up to, but not including, `to`, counted from 0. A position past the end is the end, and `from` at or past `to` gives empty `Bytes`; a negative position is a bug (13.2). `Bytes.join(parts: List(Bytes)) : Bytes` gives all the parts, in order, as one value. `to_hex : Text` encodes lowercase ASCII hex and `Bytes.from_hex(text: Text) : Option(Bytes)` decodes ASCII hex (rejecting odd lengths or non-hex characters). `to_base64url : Text` encodes unpadded URL-safe Base64 (RFC 4648 section 5), and `Bytes.from_base64url(text: Text) : Option(Bytes)` decodes it strictly (rejecting invalid characters, length `1 mod 4`, `=` padding, and non-zero trailing pad bits). `Bytes.empty : Bytes` is the zero-byte value. `Bytes.zeroed(count: Int) : Bytes` returns `count` zero bytes; a negative count or a count above 16 MiB is a bug (13.2). `Bytes.from_list(bytes: List(Byte)) : Bytes` and `to_list : List(Byte)` convert between `Bytes` and `List(Byte)`. `Bytes.from_u16_be(n: Int) : Bytes` encodes an unsigned 16-bit big-endian integer (`0` to `65535`; outside that range is a bug), `Bytes.from_u32_be(n: Int) : Bytes` encodes an unsigned 32-bit big-endian integer (`0` to `4294967295`; outside that range is a bug), and `Bytes.from_i64_be(n: Int) : Bytes` encodes a signed 64-bit big-endian two's-complement integer. `u16_be_at(offset: Int) : Option(Int)`, `u32_be_at(offset: Int) : Option(Int)` and `i64_be_at(offset: Int) : Option(Int)` decode 2, 4 or 8 big-endian bytes starting at `offset`, giving `None` when `offset < 0` or fewer than the needed bytes remain. `compare_slice_at(offset: Int, len: Int, other: Bytes) : Option(Ordering)` compares the `len` bytes starting at `offset` against `other` in unsigned byte order without allocating a slice, giving `None` when `offset < 0`, `len < 0`, or `offset + len` exceeds `size`.

**List(T)**: `size : Int`, `empty? : Bool`. `get(i: Int)`, `first` and `last : Option(T)`; `get` gives `None` for a position below 0 or past the end. `append(x: T)`, `prepend(x: T)`, `concat(other: List(T))`, `reverse`, `take(n: Int)` and `drop(n: Int)`, all `: List(T)`; `n` is at least 0, and past the end they take or drop everything. `set(i: Int, x: T)` and `remove_at(i: Int) : Option(List(T))`: `None` for a position that isn't there. `map(f: fn(T) : U) : List(U)`, `filter(pred) : List(T)`, `filter_map(f: fn(T) : Option(U)) : List(U)` (the values in the `Some`s), `flat_map(f: fn(T) : List(U)) : List(U)`, `reduce(start: A, f: fn(A, T) : A) : A` (from the left), `find(pred) : Option(T)`, `any?(pred)` and `all?(pred) : Bool`, `count(pred) : Int`, `enumerate : List((Int, T))` (from 0), `zip(other: List(U)) : List((T, U))` (as long as the shorter list). `sort_by(key: fn(T) : K)` and `sort_by_desc(key: fn(T) : K) : List(T)` where `K: Order`. `contains?(x: T) : Bool` where `T: Equal`. `sort : List(T)`, and `min` and `max : Option(T)` (the first of equal elements), where `T: Order`. `unique : List(T)`, `to_set : Set(T)` and `group_by(key: fn(T) : K) : Map(K, List(T))` (keys in the order they first appear), where `T` or `K` has `Hash`. `sum : T` where `T: Number` (`0` for an empty list). On a `List(Text)`, `join(separator: Text) : Text`; on a `List((K, V))`, `to_map : Map(K, V)`, in which a key given more than once gets its last value and keeps its first place, as with `set`.

**Map(K, V)**: `size : Int`, `empty? : Bool`, `get(key: K) : Option(V)`, `has?(key: K) : Bool`, `set(key: K, value: V)`, `remove(key: K)` and `update(key: K, default: V, f: fn(V) : V)`, all `: Map(K, V)`; `update` sets the key to `f` of its value, or of `default` when it has none. `keys : List(K)`, `values : List(V)` and `entries : List((K, V))`, in insertion order.

**Set(T)**: `size : Int`, `empty? : Bool`, `has?(x: T) : Bool`; `add(x: T)`, `remove(x: T)`, `union(other: Set(T))`, `intersection(other: Set(T))` and `difference(other: Set(T))`, all `: Set(T)`; `to_list : List(T)`. `Set.empty` is a constant: the empty set.
**Range**: `for` loops over it; `to_list : List(Int)`, `contains?(n: Int) : Bool`.
**Option(T)**: `x or default` (an operator) gives a `T`; `or_fail(e: E) : Result(T, E)`; `map(f: fn(T) : U) : Option(U)`.
**Result(T, E)**: `map(f: fn(T) : U) : Result(U, E)`, `map_error(f: fn(E) : F) : Result(T, F)`.

**Time**: `checked_add(d: Duration) : Option(Time)`, `to_text : Text`, and the operators of section 3.9. `to_text` writes RFC 3339 in UTC, with `Z`, and a fraction of a second only when there is one, as short as it can be: `2026-10-12T02:15:00Z`, `2026-10-12T02:15:00.5Z`. `Time.parse(text: Text) : Option(Time)` reads RFC 3339 text, such as `2026-10-12T04:15:00.5+02:00`: `T` or `t` between the date and the time, at most 6 digits of a fraction of a second, then `Z`, `z` or an offset, which it converts to UTC. Anything else, including a 7th fraction digit or a leap second (second 60), gives `None`. **Duration**: `in_milliseconds : Int` (rounded toward zero), `in_seconds : Decimal` (exact), `to_text : Text`.
**Args**: `list : List(Text)`, the arguments after the program's name. **Env**: `get(name: Text) : Option(Text)`.

**Console**: `print(text: Text)` and `error(text: Text)` write a line to standard output or standard error; print other values with interpolation, as in `console.print("#{count}")`. `read_line : Option(Text)` reads a line from standard input, without its line ending, `\n` or `\r\n`, and gives `None` at the input's end. Bytes that aren't valid UTF-8 become U+FFFD, the replacement character, one for each maximal invalid subpart, as Unicode recommends: the start of a valid sequence that ends too soon, or else a single byte. The bytes `a`, FF, FE, `b` read as `a`, two U+FFFD, `b`. A fake also has `printed` and `printed_errors : List(Text)`, with one entry for each line written. Using them outside tests, examples and promises is an error (section 12.4). `Console.fake() : Console`, `Console.fake_input(lines: List(Text)) : Console`.
