**Files**: `read_text(path: Text) : Result(Text, FileError)`, `read_bytes(path: Text) : Result(Bytes, FileError)`, `write_text(path: Text, text: Text)` (replaces the whole file), `write_bytes(path: Text, data: Bytes)` (replaces or creates the file with raw bytes), `append_text(path: Text, text: Text)`, `remove(path: Text)`, `rename(from: Text, to: Text)` (atomically renames one regular file to another path inside the capability's folder, replacing any existing regular file at `to`), `make_folder(folder: Text)`, each `: Result(Unit, FileError)`; `open(path: Text) : Result(Files.File, FileError)` (opens an existing regular file for random-access read/write without truncating, or creates it if missing); `list(folder: Text) : Result(List(Text), FileError)`, the names in the folder, sorted; `exists?(path: Text) : Bool`; `within(folder: Text) : Files`; `read_only : ReadFiles`. Writing, renaming or opening into a folder that doesn't exist gives `Error(NotFound(path: path))`; `make_folder` makes the folder and any missing folders above it, and succeeds if the folder already exists. `write_bytes`, `rename` and `open` refuse any symbolic link (final or intermediate) with `Error(NotAllowed(path: path))` and sync the parent folder on creation or rename. **Files.File** is an open random-access binary file capability returned by `Files.open` or `ReadFiles.open`, closed when dropped. Up to 64 files may be open at once; opening another is a bug (13.2). `read_at(offset: Int, count: Int) : Result(Bytes, FileError)` reads up to `count` bytes starting at `offset` (giving shorter or empty `Bytes` at or past the end; a negative `offset`, negative `count`, or `count` above 16 MiB is a bug). `write_at(offset: Int, data: Bytes) : Result(Unit, FileError)` writes all of `data` at `offset`, zero-extending if `offset` is past the current end (a negative `offset` is a bug). `size : Result(Int, FileError)` gives the current byte length. `truncate(size: Int) : Result(Unit, FileError)` shrinks or zero-extends the file to `size` bytes (a negative `size` is a bug). `sync : Result(Unit, FileError)` flushes the file's bytes to durable storage. `lock_shared : Result(Unit, FileError)`, `lock_exclusive : Result(Unit, FileError)` and `unlock : Result(Unit, FileError)` acquire and release advisory file locks bound to the open handle (BSD `flock` on real files, released automatically when the handle is dropped; in-memory fakes return `Error(Failed(path: path, reason: ...))` on conflicting handles instead of deadlocking, and `unlock` succeeds on an unlocked handle). On a read-only handle returned by `ReadFiles.open`, `write_at`, `truncate`, `sync` and `lock_exclusive` return `Error(NotAllowed(path: path))` without touching the file, while `read_at`, `size`, `lock_shared` and `unlock` work normally. `entries(folder: Text) : Result(List(Entry), FileError)` gives the folder's entries in `list`'s order, each an `Entry(name: Text, kind: EntryKind)` whose kind is `File`, `Folder`, `Link` or `Other`; a link is reported, never followed. `walk(folder: Text) : Result(List(Entry), FileError)` gives every entry below the folder, each named by its path from the folder: a folder's entries in `list`'s order, each folder followed by what's inside it. It doesn't enter links, and stops at the first folder it can't read. A capability from `within` or `read_only` holds its folder open while it's used, and having too many open at once is a bug (13.2). `Files.in_memory(files: Map(Text, Text)) : Files`. In such a fake, files are stored as raw bytes (so `write_bytes`, `rename`, `open` and `Files.File` operations behave identically to real files, while `read_text` gives `Error(NotText(path: path))` on non-UTF-8 bytes), the folders are those its files are in, those `make_folder` made, and those whose last file was removed, as on a disk, and `list` and `entries` give the names directly inside a folder, each subfolder once. Files that make one path both a file and a folder, as `{"a": "x", "a/b": "y"}` do, are a bug (13.2). So are keys that aren't plain relative paths, such as `"/a"`, `"./a"`, `"a/"` or `"a//b"`. **ReadFiles** has `read_text`, `read_bytes`, `open` (opening an existing confined regular file read-only as a `Files.File`, giving `Error(NotFound(path: path))` if missing), `list`, `entries`, `walk`, `exists?` and `within`. Paths are relative and use `/`; `"."` is the capability's own folder, and no path can leave it. Given a path that would leave the folder, such as `"../a.txt"`, reading, writing, removing and listing give `Error(NotAllowed(path: path))`, and `exists?` gives `false`. Calling `within` with such a path gives a capability that reaches nothing: every call on it that returns a `Result` gives `Error(NotAllowed(path: path))`, and `exists?` on it gives `false`. A path may pass through symbolic links that stay inside the folder, and every operation follows them; a path through an absolute link, or one that leads outside, is refused in the same way, and one through more than 40 links gives `Error(Failed(path: path, reason: "too many links"))`. `remove` removes a link itself, never what it points to. Listing a file, or making a folder where a file is, gives `Error(Failed(path: path, reason: "not a folder"))`, and reading, writing, appending to or removing a folder gives `Error(Failed(path: path, reason: "is a folder"))`.

**FileError**: `NotFound(path: Text)`, `NotAllowed(path: Text)`, `NotText(path: Text)`, when `read_text` finds a file that isn't valid UTF-8, and `Failed(path: Text, reason: Text)`. Its text forms are `PATH: no such file`, `PATH: not allowed`, `PATH: not text` and `PATH: REASON`, as in `notes/a.md: no such file`.

**Clock**: `now : Time`, a bug if the system's clock is outside the years 1 to 9999; `sleep(duration: Duration)`, which waits on a real clock and advances a fixed clock by `duration` (a bug if `duration` is negative or moves the time outside the years 1 to 9999); `Clock.fixed(time: Time) : Clock`. **Random**: `int(low: Int, high: Int) : Int`, from `low` up to, but not including, `high`, which must be greater; `Random.seeded(seed: Int) : Random`. **SecureRandom**: `bytes(count: Int) : Bytes` draws `count` cryptographically secure random bytes (`0` to `65536`; outside that range is a bug, 13.2) from the operating system CSPRNG, failing closed on error; `SecureRandom.seeded(seed: Int) : SecureRandom` makes a deterministic fake in tests, examples and promises. **Args** and **Env** fakes: `Args.of(list: List(Text))`, `Env.of(map: Map(Text, Text))`.

A connection has no `close`: it closes when the program no longer holds it. A port outside 1 to 65,535, a `most` below 1 or above 1,048,576, and more than 64 connections open at once are bugs (13.2).

**NetworkError**: `UnknownHost(host: Text)`, for a name that doesn't exist, is empty, is longer than 253 bytes or holds a NUL character; `Refused(host: Text, port: Int)`; `TimedOut`; `Closed`, when the other side reset the connection, closed it during a TLS handshake, or closed it before a `send` or TLS record finished; `Broken(reason: Text)`, with the system's or TLS protocol's reason for anything else; and `Certificate(reason: Text)`, when TLS certificate or host verification fails. Its cases are written with `Network.` in front, in expressions and in patterns, as in `Network.Refused(host: "example.org", port: 80)`, so a program may give its own types cases with these names. Its text forms are those of section 9.2, as in `Refused(host: "example.org", port: 80)`.

A key of `peers` is a host and a port, as in `"example.org:80"` or `"example.org:443"`, and its value maps the exact bytes a connection sends to the bytes it then receives. `connect` or `connect_secure` to a host and port that `peers` lacks gives `Error(Network.UnknownHost(host: host))`. A connection collects what it is sent, and its first `receive` looks up everything sent so far. With a reply, `receive` hands it out, at most `most` bytes at a time, and then gives empty `Bytes`. With none, every `receive` gives `Error(Network.Broken(reason: reason))`. The reason quotes the first line sent, and, when `peers` holds a request that starts with the same lines, the first line that differs. A `send` after the first `receive` gives `Error(Network.Closed)`. A fake opens no connection, runs no TLS and reads no clock: `within` is ignored, and a fake's connections don't count toward the limit. The `Network` that `mo test` makes for a promise has no peers. `Network.fake_scripted(scripts: List((Text, Text, List(Network.FakeReply)))) : Network` scripts an ordered queue of `Network.FakeReply` outcomes matched by `(method, url_prefix)` (`Network.Respond(response: Http.Response)`, `Network.Fail(error: NetworkError)` and `Network.TruncateAfter(bytes: Int)` closing the response stream mid-body after `bytes` payload bytes), obeying `allow_hosts` narrowing, repeating a target's final reply once exhausted, and returning `Error(Network.Refused(host: host, port: port))` for unmatched targets, and `Network.recorded_calls(network: Network) : List(Network.RecordedCall)` returns the `Network.RecordedCall(method: Text, url: Text, headers: List((Text, Text)), body: Bytes)` entries sent on a fake `Network` in order.

An object keeps its keys in the document's order, and a key given twice is an error. **Http**, with `use Http`, is an HTTP/1.1 client over a `Network`. A program builds a `Request` a step at a time and sends it, and gets a `Response`:

`Http.get(url: Text)` and `Http.post(url: Text)` give a `Request`, and `Http.request(method: Text, url: Text)` gives one with any other method. It starts with no headers, an empty body, a timeout of 30 seconds and a `body_limit` of 16,777,216 bytes. `request.header(name: Text, value: Text)` adds a header. `request.query(name: Text, value: Text)` adds a query parameter to the URL, and writes every byte of the name and the value as `%` and two hexadecimal digits except ASCII letters, digits, `-`, `.`, `_` and `~`. `request.form(pairs: List((Text, Text)))` sets the body to `pairs` written with that same percent-encoding as `name=value` joined by `&`, with the content type `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`; `request.json(value: Json)` sets the body to `value` as compact JSON with the content type `application/json`, and `request.text(text: Text)` sets it to `text` with `text/plain; charset=utf-8`; each replaces a `Content-Type` header the request already had. `request.within(timeout: Duration)` sets the timeout, and `request.max_body(bytes: Int)` sets `body_limit`. Each gives a new `Request`, and none of them fails: `send` reports a bad URL, method or header.

`request.send(network: Network) : Result(Response, HttpError)` opens one connection with the request's timeout as its `within`, writes the request, reads the response to its end, and lets the connection close. A URL is `http://` or `https://`, a host, then an optional `:` and port from 1 to 65,535, an optional path and an optional query. Without a port it is 80 for `http://` and 443 for `https://`, and without a path it is `/`. A URL of any other form, or one that holds a space, a control character, a `#`, or a `@` in its host, gives `Error(BadUrl(url))`. `send` opens its connection with `connect` for `http://` and `connect_secure` for `https://`. A method that isn't ASCII letters gives `Error(BadHeader(name))` with the method as the name. So does a header whose name is empty or holds a space, a `:` or a control character, whose value holds a control character, or whose name is `Host`, `Connection`, `Content-Length` or `Transfer-Encoding` in any case, with the header's name. After any of these errors nothing was sent, so nothing a program passes can add a line to a request. The client writes its own headers first: `Host`, then `Connection: close`, then `Content-Length` when the body isn't empty or the method is neither `GET` nor `HEAD`. The program's headers follow, sorted by name without regard to case, and headers with the same name keep the order they were added in.

A response's body ends where its `Content-Length` says, where its chunks end when its `Transfer-Encoding` is `chunked`, and otherwise where the server closes the connection. The response to a `HEAD` request and one with status 204 or 304 have an empty body. Any status is a response: 404 and 500 are not errors, and a status from 100 to 199 is read like any other. `send` follows no redirect, retries nothing, keeps no cookie, uses no proxy, reuses no connection and asks for no compression. Headers longer than 65,536 bytes, a status line or header line that is malformed, a line that doesn't end with a carriage return and a line feed or that holds a control character other than a tab, another transfer encoding or more than one, and a connection closed before the response was whole each give `Error(BadResponse(reason))`. A body longer than the request's `body_limit` (16,777,216 bytes unless `max_body` changed it) gives `Error(TooLarge(limit: limit))`. A failure of the network gives `Error(Unreachable(error))`, as in `Unreachable(Network.TimedOut)`. An `HttpError`'s text forms are those of section 9.2.

`response.ok? : Bool` is true for a status from 200 to 299. `response.header(name: Text) : Option(Text)` gives the first header with that name, without regard to case, and `response.headers_named(name: Text) : List(Text)` gives every header value with that name in response order. `response.text : Option(Text)` gives the body when it is UTF-8. `response.json : Result(Json, HttpError)` parses the body: `Error(NotJson(error))` holds `Json.parse`'s error, and a body that isn't UTF-8 gives `Error(BadResponse(reason))`.
